title: Rotate Image
corePattern: In-Place Matrix Transformation via Transpose + Reversal / Cyclic Permutation
interviewTips: Ask if rotation must be in-place (O(1) extra space) and if matrix is guaranteed n x n square.
Clarify direction: clockwise 90 degrees vs counter-clockwise, and whether to modify in place (void) vs return new matrix.
Trade-off: extra-matrix copy is simplest to derive but O(n^2) space; transpose+reverse achieves O(1) space with same O(n^2) time and is least error-prone to code.
Edge-case tip: test n=1 (no-op) and n=2 (single 4-cycle); for transpose loop use j=i+1 to avoid double-swap, and for reverse use n/2 swaps.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Extra Matrix Copy
approaches.intuition: Rotating clockwise moves element at (r,c) to (c, n-1-r). If we can use extra space, just compute destination for every cell from a snapshot copy.
approaches.theory: Clockwise rotation is the mapping old[i][j] -> new[j][n-1-i], equivalently new[i][j] = old[n-1-j][i]. Copy the matrix first so reads are not overwritten, then write each position using that formula. This proves correctness by direct coordinate transformation.

timeComplexity.explanation: Visit each of n*n cells once to copy and once to write. n is matrix dimension.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Extra n x n copy of matrix to avoid overwrite during mapping.

edgeCases: Already rotated or large n up to constraints still O(n^2)

approaches.name: Approach 2: Transpose + Reverse Rows
approaches.intuition: A clockwise rotation equals a transpose across main diagonal followed by mirroring left-right (reverse each row). Both steps are in-place.
approaches.theory: Transpose swaps (i,j) with (j,i). Reversing each row maps (i,j) to (i,n-1-j). Composition gives (i,j) -> (j,i) -> (j,n-1-i) which is exactly clockwise rotation mapping. Transpose needs only upper triangle j>i to avoid double swap; reverse needs n/2 swaps per row.

timeComplexity.explanation: Transpose touches ~n^2/2 pairs + n^2/2 reversals = O(n^2). Each cell moved O(1) times.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only constant extra variables for swapping; modifies matrix in place.

edgeCases: n=1: transpose and reverse are no-ops
Must loop j from i+1 not 0 to avoid swapping back

approaches.name: Approach 3: Layer-by-Layer 4-Way Swap
approaches.intuition: Rotation moves 4 cells in a cycle: top -> right -> bottom -> left -> top. Process outer layer inward, rotating each group of 4 directly without transpose.
approaches.theory: For layer with first=L and last=n-1-L, cells (L,i), (n-1-(i-L),L) wait correct cycle is top(L,i) <- left(n-1-offset,L) <- bottom(n-1,n-1-offset) <- right(i,n-1) <- top. Saving top temp allows 4 assignments in cycle. There are n//2 layers and n-1-2*L groups per layer, covering all n^2 cells exactly once.

code.python:
from typing import List
class Solution:
    def rotate(self, matrix: List[List[int]]) -> None:
        n = len(matrix)
        for layer in range(n // 2):
            first = layer
            last = n - 1 - layer
            for i in range(first, last):
                offset = i - first
                top = matrix[first][i]
                matrix[first][i] = matrix[last - offset][first]
                matrix[last - offset][first] = matrix[last][last - offset]
                matrix[last][last - offset] = matrix[i][last]
                matrix[i][last] = top

timeComplexity.explanation: Each cell belongs to exactly one 4-cycle and is moved once; total cycles ~n^2/4.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only one temp variable top per 4-swap; in-place by layers.

edgeCases: n odd: center cell (e.g., 5 in 3x3) never moves, layers = n//2 handles it
n=2: one layer, one cycle of 4 cells
Off-by-one: inner loop must be i < last not <= last to avoid re-rotating corner
